title: Milner’s completeness problem
formal: Historical question, resolved affirmatively: for all regular expressions \(e,f\) over any finite action alphabet, does bisimilarity of their process interpretations imply that \(e=f\) is derivable in Milner’s proof system \(\mathrm{Mil}\)? Grabmayer’s LICS 2022 completeness theorem proves this implication for the full expression language defined below.

source_formulation.text: Of particular interest is an open problem posed by Milner in [25], which consists of showing that a certain set of axioms are complete w.r.t. […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 12

context:
Regular expressions can denote either languages or process behaviors. Bisimilarity compares which actions remain available after each step and preserves termination. Equality of accepted words alone is too coarse for this completeness question.

The source cites the earlier completeness theorem for one-free expressions and describes the full Milner problem as open. Its discussion of GKAT and a uniqueness axiom concerns a different expression language and should not replace the target here.

Grabmayer’s Theorem 5.1 states completeness for Milner’s system on regular expressions, including 0, 1 and unary star. Soundness was already known. Together these facts identify derivable equality with bisimilarity for the stated process interpretation.

Kappé and Schmid’s 2025 paper explicitly attributes the resolution of Milner’s problem to Grabmayer, then studies a broader family of skip-free star algebras. This corroborates that the 2021 open-status label is stale.
why: The result gives a complete algebraic proof calculus for behavioral equivalence of regular processes. It connects operational program semantics with finite symbolic derivations and resolves a long-standing distinction between regular-language identities and branching behavior.
status_note: Checked the original conclusion, the published LICS 2022 record and corrected report Definitions 3.5–3.6 and Theorem 5.1, plus the 2025 follow-up’s explicit account of the resolution. The result covers the full language and the guarded fixed-point rule. This editorial review checks the theorem’s scope and publication, not an independent reconstruction or formal verification of its proof.

sentences: Regular expressions here describe branching processes with deadlock and successful termination.
Two expressions are equivalent when their transitions and termination behavior match by bisimulation.
Milner’s rules give a sound way to prove such equivalences.
The question was whether every equivalence has a finite proof in that system.
Grabmayer’s published 2022 theorem answers yes for the full language.

references.title: Guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests: Coequations, Coinduction, and Completeness
references.authors: Schmid, Todd; Kappé, Tobias; Kozen, Dexter; Silva, Alexandra
references.locator: Explicit open question on PDF page 12

definitions:
Fix a finite set \(A\) of action symbols. Expressions are finite terms
\[e::=0\mid1\mid a\mid(e+e)\mid(e\cdot e)\mid e^{*},\qquad a\in A.\]
Here 0 is deadlock, 1 is successful immediate termination, \(+\) is nondeterministic choice, multiplication is sequential composition, and star is iteration.

Define the immediate-termination predicate \(e\downarrow\) recursively. It holds for 1 and every \(e^{*}\), for \(e+f\) exactly when at least one summand terminates, and for \(e\cdot f\) exactly when both factors terminate. It does not hold for 0 or an action.

For each action \(a\), the transition relation \(\xrightarrow{a}\) is the least relation generated by the following rules. There is a transition \(a\xrightarrow{a}1\). Every transition of either summand is a transition of their sum. If \(e\xrightarrow{a}g\), then \(e\cdot f\xrightarrow{a}g\cdot f\) and \(e^{*}\xrightarrow{a}g\cdot e^{*}\). If \(e\downarrow\) and \(f\xrightarrow{a}g\), then \(e\cdot f\xrightarrow{a}g\). There are no other transitions.

A bisimulation is a relation \(B\) on expressions such that, whenever \((e,f)\in B\), they have the same termination predicate and each action transition from either expression can be matched by a transition with the same label from the other, with the resulting expressions again related by \(B\). The expressions are bisimilar if some such relation contains their pair. This is strong bisimilarity with observable successful termination. The constant 1 is not an action label or a silent transition in this semantics.

The proof system has these equation schemata, for arbitrary expressions \(e,f,g\):
\[\begin{aligned}
e+(f+g)&=(e+f)+g,&e+0&=e,\\
e+f&=f+e,&e+e&=e,\\
e\cdot(f\cdot g)&=(e\cdot f)\cdot g,\\
(e+f)\cdot g&=e\cdot g+f\cdot g,\\
1\cdot e&=e,&e\cdot1&=e,&0\cdot e&=0,\\
e^{*}&=1+e\cdot e^{*},&
e^{*}&=(1+e)^{*}.
\end{aligned}\]
It permits reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of equality, and replacement of equals within each expression constructor. In addition, its fixed-point rule is
\[\frac{e=f\cdot e+g}{e=f^{*}\cdot g}\qquad\text{provided }f\not\downarrow.\]
The premise must itself be derivable; the side condition means that \(f\) cannot terminate immediately, as computed by the recursive predicate above. A proof is a finite derivation using these schemata and rules.

The system includes successful termination and unary star. Dropping 1 and replacing unary star by a binary iteration operator gives the separate one-free fragment. Dropping the fixed-point rule gives only the equational fragment, which is not the system in the question. Familiar language identities such as unrestricted left distributivity and \(e\cdot0=0\) must not be added: they need not preserve this branching process semantics.
answer_criterion: The historical target is a completeness proof for every pair of bisimilar expressions in the full language and exactly the displayed proof system. A theorem only about equality of accepted languages, about a restricted fragment, or about a stronger proof system would not suffice. The cited theorem establishes the required implication.
